summary.text: An equation joins two expressions with an equals sign to say they have the same value.
Solving one means finding which values of the unknowns make the equality true; those values are its solutions.
An equation stays balanced, like a scale, when you do the same operation to both sides.

facts.label: Identity
facts.value: True for all values of the variables

facts.label: Usual letters
facts.value: Unknowns use x, y, z; coefficients use a, b, c

facts.label: Two sides
facts.value: Called the left-hand side and right-hand side

items.prompt: A balance scale holds 5 apples in each pan. You take 2 apples out of the left pan. What keeps it level?

options.label: Add 2 apples to the right pan
Leave it, since a scale fixes itself
Take 2 apples out of the right pan too
Take every apple out of the right pan

items.explain: An equation, like a scale, stays balanced when the same change is made on both sides.

items.prompt: Maya tests an equation with many different numbers for its variable, and every one works. Which kind of equation is it, if it holds for all values?

options.label: An identity
A conditional equation
A coefficient
An unknown

items.explain: An identity is true for all values of the variables, while a conditional equation holds only for particular values.

items.prompt: Which number is a solution of the equation x + 3 = 7?
items.explain: A solution is a value of the unknown that makes the equality true, and 4 + 3 equals 7.

items.prompt: You have the equation 2x = 10 and want to keep it balanced. Which step is allowed?

options.label: Divide only the left side by 2
Add 2 to the left side only
Change the sign on one side only
Divide both sides by 2

items.explain: Multiplying or dividing both sides by the same non-zero quantity keeps an equation balanced.

items.prompt: Someone solves x = 1, then squares both sides to get a new equation. What can go wrong?

options.label: The new equation can have an extra solution the old one lacked
The new equation must have exactly the same solutions
The new equation can have no solutions at all
The new equation turns the unknown into a constant

items.explain: Squaring turns x = 1 into x² = 1, which brings in the extraneous solution x = −1.

items.prompt: Which move turns any equation into one with only zero on one side?

options.label: Multiply both sides by zero
Subtract the other side from both sides
Erase one of the two sides
Divide both sides by the other side

items.explain: Subtracting the right-hand side from both sides makes every equation equivalent to one with zero on the right.

pack.title: Do the same to both sides
pack.question: What can you do to an equation without breaking it?

beats.title: Do the same to both sides
beats.hook: A scale that tips the moment you cheat is a surprisingly good way to learn algebra.

beats.prompt: A scale holds equal grain in both pans and balances. You scoop some grain out of the left pan. What puts it back in balance?
beats.explain: An equation stays balanced when the same operation is done on each side, just as removing equal grain from both pans does.

choices.label: Add more grain to the right pan
choices.feedback: It sounds like evening things up, but that makes the right side heavier, not equal.

choices.label: Do nothing, since equal pans stay equal
choices.feedback: They were equal only before one pan lost grain.

choices.label: Empty the right pan completely
choices.feedback: That removes far more than was taken from the left.

choices.label: Scoop the same amount out of the right pan

beats.prompt: Match each word to what it means.

right.label: A value of the unknown that makes the equality true
True for all values of the variables
A variable the equation is to be solved for

beats.explain: Unknowns are what you solve for, solutions satisfy the equality, and equations are identities or conditional depending on how many values work.

beats.prompt: Sort each move by how safe it is.

left.label: Add the same amount to both sides
Multiply both sides by a non-zero number

beats.explain: Adding or multiplying by a non-zero quantity keeps balance, but applying a function can add extra solutions, or lose solutions where it is undefined, as 1/x is for x = 0.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?

steps.text: Start with x = 1, which is solved by x = 1.
Square both sides to get x² = 1.
Since the new equation came from the old one, it has no new solutions.
So we can square both sides freely when solving.

beats.explain: Squaring brings in the extraneous solution x = −1, so the new equation has solutions the old one did not.

beats.idea: An equation stays true when you treat both sides alike, but some moves can slip in extra answers.

paragraphs.heading: What an equation is
paragraphs.text: An equation states that two expressions are equal, with the equals sign = placed between them. The expression on the left is called the left-hand side, and the one on the right is the right-hand side. In English, any well-formed formula made of two expressions joined by an equals sign counts as an equation. Other languages can draw the line differently: French keeps équation for statements with one or more variables and uses égalité where no variable is needed. The = sign itself was invented in 1557 by Robert Recorde, who felt nothing could be more equal than two parallel straight lines of the same length.

paragraphs.heading: Unknowns and solutions
paragraphs.text: Many equations contain variables. Solving such an equation means finding the values of those variables that make the equality true. The variables you solve for are called unknowns, and the values that work are called solutions. Other terms in the equation are taken as known and are usually called constants, coefficients or parameters. By habit, unknowns get letters from the end of the alphabet, such as x, y and z, while coefficients get letters from the start, as in the general quadratic equation ax² + bx + c = 0.

paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of equation
paragraphs.text: Equations come in two kinds. An identity holds for every value of its variables. A conditional equation holds only for particular values of them.

paragraphs.heading: Like a balance scale
paragraphs.text: A helpful picture is a balance scale with two pans. Put equal weights in the pans and the scale sits level, just as the two sides of an equation are equal. Take some grain out of one pan and you must take the same amount out of the other to keep it level. In the same way, an equation stays balanced when you do the same operation to both sides. If the two sides are not equal, the tipped scale stands for an inequality instead.

paragraphs.heading: Moves that keep the balance
paragraphs.text: Several standard moves follow from this rule. You can add or subtract the same quantity on both sides, which shows that any equation can be rewritten with zero on the right-hand side. You can multiply or divide both sides by a quantity that is not zero. You can also rewrite one side using an identity, for example by expanding a product or factoring a sum. These moves are the basis of most elementary ways of solving equations, and of some less elementary ones such as Gaussian elimination.

paragraphs.heading: A warning about extra solutions
paragraphs.text: Applying some other function to both sides needs more care. The new equation keeps all the old solutions but may pick up extra ones, called extraneous solutions. For example, x = 1 has the solution x = 1, but squaring both sides gives x² = 1, which also lets in x = −1. And if the function is undefined at some values, as 1/x is at x = 0, solutions at those values can be lost.
